Let ≈₁ and ≤₁ be the equivalence and partial order given by the hypothesis IsPartialOrder, so ≈₁ is an equivalence relation, ≤₁ is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric with respect to ≈₁, and ≤₁ respects ≈₁ in both arguments. Write a <₁ b for "a ≤₁ b and not a ≈₁ b". Take p ≤ₗₑₓ q to mean: p₁ <₁ q₁, or p₁ ≈₁ q₁ and p₂ ≤₂ q₂.
2. [lemma/hard] For a, b, c in A, if a <₁ b and b ≤₁ c, then a <₁ c. Proof: from a ≤₁ b and b ≤₁ c, transitivity gives a ≤₁ c. Suppose, for contradiction, that a ≈₁ c. Since b ≤₁ c and c ≈₁ a, respect of ≤₁ gives b ≤₁ a. Together with a ≤₁ b, antisymmetry gives a ≈₁ b, which contradicts a <₁ b. Hence not a ≈₁ c, and so a <₁ c.
3. [lemma/hard] For a, b, c in A, if a ≤₁ b and b <₁ c, then a <₁ c. Proof: from a ≤₁ b and b ≤₁ c (which follows from b <₁ c), transitivity gives a ≤₁ c. Suppose, for contradiction, that a ≈₁ c. Since a ≤₁ b and c ≈₁ a, respect of ≤₁ gives c ≤₁ b. Together with b ≤₁ c, antisymmetry gives b ≈₁ c, which contradicts b <₁ c. Hence not a ≈₁ c, and so a <₁ c.
4. [case] Assume p ≤ₗₑₓ q and q ≤ₗₑₓ r. We split on the two ways p ≤ₗₑₓ q can hold, and then on the two ways q ≤ₗₑₓ r can hold.
5. [case] Case 1: p₁ <₁ q₁. Subcase 1a: q₁ <₁ r₁. Then p₁ <₁ r₁ by the lemma ltLeTrans, applied to p₁ <₁ q₁ and q₁ ≤₁ r₁. So p ≤ₗₑₓ r, since its first disjunct holds.
6. [case] Case 1, subcase 1b: q₁ ≈₁ r₁ and q₂ ≤₂ r₂. Since q₁ ≈₁ r₁, we have q₁ ≤₁ r₁. Then p₁ <₁ r₁ by the lemma ltLeTrans, applied to p₁ <₁ q₁ and q₁ ≤₁ r₁. So p ≤ₗₑₓ r, since its first disjunct holds.
7. [case] Case 2: p₁ ≈₁ q₁ and p₂ ≤₂ q₂. Subcase 2a: q₁ <₁ r₁. Since p₁ ≈₁ q₁, we have p₁ ≤₁ q₁. Then p₁ <₁ r₁ by the lemma leLtTrans, applied to p₁ ≤₁ q₁ and q₁ <₁ r₁. So p ≤ₗₑₓ r, since its first disjunct holds.

-- Definition

×-Lex : (_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁) (_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂) (_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃) →
        Rel (A × B) _
×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_ = Strict.×-Lex _≈₁_ (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_) _≤₂_

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Properties

×-reflexive : (_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁) (_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂)
              {_≈₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃} (_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₄) →
              _≈₂_ ⇒ _≤₂_ →
              (Pointwise _≈₁_ _≈₂_) ⇒ (×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_)

  Strict.×-reflexive _≈₁_ (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_) _≤₂_ refl₂

module _ {_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁} {_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂} {_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃} where

  private
    _≤ₗₑₓ_ = ×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_

  ×-transitive : IsPartialOrder _≈₁_ _≤₁_ → Transitive _≤₂_ →
                 Transitive _≤ₗₑₓ_
  ×-transitive po₁ trans₂ =
    Strict.×-transitive {_≈₁_ = _≈₁_} {_<₂_ = _≤₂_}
      isEquivalence (Conv.<-resp-≈ _ _ isEquivalence ≤-resp-≈)
      (Conv.<-trans _ _ po₁)
      trans₂
    where open IsPartialOrder po₁

  ×-decidable : Decidable _≈₁_ → Decidable _≤₁_ → Decidable _≤₂_ →
                Decidable _≤ₗₑₓ_
  ×-decidable dec-≈₁ dec-≤₁ dec-≤₂ =
    Strict.×-decidable dec-≈₁ (Conv.<-decidable _ _ dec-≈₁ dec-≤₁)
                       dec-≤₂

module _ {_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁} {_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂}
         {_≈₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃} {_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₄}
         where

  private
    _≤ₗₑₓ_ = ×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_
    _≋_    = Pointwise _≈₁_ _≈₂_

  ×-antisymmetric : IsPartialOrder _≈₁_ _≤₁_ → Antisymmetric _≈₂_ _≤₂_ →
                   Antisymmetric _≋_ _≤ₗₑₓ_
  ×-antisymmetric po₁ antisym₂ =
    Strict.×-antisymmetric {_≈₁_ = _≈₁_} {_<₂_ = _≤₂_}
       ≈-sym₁ irrefl₁ asym₁ antisym₂
    where
    open IsPartialOrder po₁
    open Eq renaming (refl to ≈-refl₁; sym to ≈-sym₁)

    irrefl₁ : Irreflexive _≈₁_ (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_)
    irrefl₁ = Conv.<-irrefl _≈₁_ _≤₁_

    asym₁ : Asymmetric (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_)

                           ≈-refl₁ (Conv.<-trans _ _ po₁) irrefl₁

  ×-respects₂ : IsEquivalence _≈₁_ →
                _≤₁_ Respects₂ _≈₁_ → _≤₂_ Respects₂ _≈₂_ →
                _≤ₗₑₓ_ Respects₂ _≋_

    Strict.×-respects₂ eq₁ (Conv.<-resp-≈ _ _ eq₁ resp₁) resp₂

-- the left-hand relation is a (non-strict) partial order.

module Data.Product.Relation.Binary.Lex.NonStrict where

open import Data.Product.Base using (_×_; _,_; proj₁; proj₂)
open import Data.Product.Relation.Binary.Pointwise.NonDependent as Pointwise
  using (Pointwise)
import Data.Product.Relation.Binary.Lex.Strict as Strict
open import Data.Sum.Base using (inj₁; inj₂)
open import Level using (Level)
open import Relation.Binary.Core using (Rel; _⇒_)
open import Relation.Binary.Bundles
  using (Poset; DecTotalOrder; TotalOrder)
open import Relation.Binary.Structures
  using (IsPartialOrder; IsEquivalence; IsTotalOrder; IsDecTotalOrder)
open import Relation.Binary.Definitions
  using (Transitive; Symmetric; Decidable; Antisymmetric; Total; Trichotomous
        ; Irreflexive; Asymmetric; _Respects₂_; tri<; tri>; tri≈)
open import Relation.Binary.Consequences
import Relation.Binary.Construct.NonStrictToStrict as Conv


private
  variable
    a b ℓ₁ ℓ₂ ℓ₃ ℓ₄ : Level
    A : Set a
    B : Set b

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Definition

×-Lex : (_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁) (_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂) (_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃) →
        Rel (A × B) _
×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_ = Strict.×-Lex _≈₁_ (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_) _≤₂_

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Properties

×-reflexive : (_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁) (_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂)
              {_≈₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃} (_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₄) →
              _≈₂_ ⇒ _≤₂_ →
              (Pointwise _≈₁_ _≈₂_) ⇒ (×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_)
×-reflexive _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_ refl₂ =
  Strict.×-reflexive _≈₁_ (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_) _≤₂_ refl₂

module _ {_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁} {_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂} {_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃} where

  private
    _≤ₗₑₓ_ = ×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_

  ×-transitive : IsPartialOrder _≈₁_ _≤₁_ → Transitive _≤₂_ →
                 Transitive _≤ₗₑₓ_
  ×-transitive po₁ trans₂ =
    Strict.×-transitive {_≈₁_ = _≈₁_} {_<₂_ = _≤₂_}
      isEquivalence (Conv.<-resp-≈ _ _ isEquivalence ≤-resp-≈)
      (Conv.<-trans _ _ po₁)
      trans₂
    where open IsPartialOrder po₁

  ×-decidable : Decidable _≈₁_ → Decidable _≤₁_ → Decidable _≤₂_ →
                Decidable _≤ₗₑₓ_
  ×-decidable dec-≈₁ dec-≤₁ dec-≤₂ =
    Strict.×-decidable dec-≈₁ (Conv.<-decidable _ _ dec-≈₁ dec-≤₁)
                       dec-≤₂

module _ {_≈₁_ : Rel A ℓ₁} {_≤₁_ : Rel A ℓ₂}
         {_≈₂_ : Rel B ℓ₃} {_≤₂_ : Rel B ℓ₄}
         where

  private
    _≤ₗₑₓ_ = ×-Lex _≈₁_ _≤₁_ _≤₂_
    _≋_    = Pointwise _≈₁_ _≈₂_

  ×-antisymmetric : IsPartialOrder _≈₁_ _≤₁_ → Antisymmetric _≈₂_ _≤₂_ →
                   Antisymmetric _≋_ _≤ₗₑₓ_
  ×-antisymmetric po₁ antisym₂ =
    Strict.×-antisymmetric {_≈₁_ = _≈₁_} {_<₂_ = _≤₂_}
       ≈-sym₁ irrefl₁ asym₁ antisym₂
    where
    open IsPartialOrder po₁
    open Eq renaming (refl to ≈-refl₁; sym to ≈-sym₁)

    irrefl₁ : Irreflexive _≈₁_ (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_)
    irrefl₁ = Conv.<-irrefl _≈₁_ _≤₁_

    asym₁ : Asymmetric (Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_)
    asym₁ = trans∧irr⇒asym {_≈_ = _≈₁_}
                           ≈-refl₁ (Conv.<-trans _ _ po₁) irrefl₁

  ×-respects₂ : IsEquivalence _≈₁_ →
                _≤₁_ Respects₂ _≈₁_ → _≤₂_ Respects₂ _≈₂_ →
                _≤ₗₑₓ_ Respects₂ _≋_

    Strict.×-respects₂ eq₁ (Conv.<-resp-≈ _ _ eq₁ resp₁) resp₂


------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Structures

  -- dsp: lemmas
  postulate
    ltLeTrans : IsPartialOrder _≈₁_ _≤₁_ → _≤₁_ Respects₂ _≈₁_ → {a b c : A} → Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_ a b → b ≤₁ c → Conv._<_ _≈₁_ _≤₁_ a c

  ×-lex-trans : IsPartialOrder _≈₁_ _≤₁_ → _≤₁_ Respects₂ _≈₁_ → Transitive _≤₂_ → ∀ {p q r : A × B} → p ≤ₗₑₓ q → q ≤ₗₑₓ r → p ≤ₗₑₓ r

  -- Case 1, subcase 1a: p₁ <₁ q₁ and q₁ <₁ r₁ give p₁ <₁ r₁ by ltLeTrans, so p ≤ₗₑₓ r since its first disjunct holds.
  ×-lex-trans po₁ resp₁ trans₂ (inj₁ pq) (inj₁ qr) = {!!}
  -- Case 1, subcase 1b: q₁ ≈₁ r₁ and q₂ ≤₂ r₂. Since q₁ ≈₁ r₁, we have q₁ ≤₁ r₁. Then p₁ <₁ r₁ by ltLeTrans, so p ≤ₗₑₓ r since its first disjunct holds.
  ×-lex-trans po₁ resp₁ trans₂ (inj₁ pq) (inj₂ (qe , ql)) = {!!}
  -- Case 2, subcase 2a: p₁ ≈₁ q₁ and p₂ ≤₂ q₂, with q₁ <₁ r₁. Since p₁ ≈₁ q₁, we have p₁ ≤₁ q₁. Then p₁ <₁ r₁ by leLtTrans, so p ≤ₗₑₓ r since its first disjunct holds.
  ×-lex-trans po₁ resp₁ trans₂ (inj₂ (pe , pl)) (inj₁ qr) = {!!}
  -- Case 2, subcase 2b: q₁ ≈₁ r₁ and q₂ ≤₂ r₂. From p₁ ≈₁ q₁ and q₁ ≈₁ r₁, transitivity of ≈₁ gives p₁ ≈₁ r₁. From p₂ ≤₂ q₂ and q₂ ≤₂ r₂, transitivity of ≤₂ gives p₂ ≤₂ r₂. So p ≤ₗₑₓ r via the second disjunct.
  ×-lex-trans po₁ resp₁ trans₂ (inj₂ (pe , pl)) (inj₂ (qe , ql)) = {!!}

2. [step] Assume p ≤ₗₑₓ q and q ≤ₗₑₓ p. We split into cases according to the two alternatives given by p ≤ₗₑₓ q.
3. [case] Case A: a <₁ c. We show this case is impossible. From a <₁ c we have a ≤₁ c and a ≉₁ c. Now we use q ≤ₗₑₓ p, which gives either c <₁ a, or c ≈₁ a and d ≤₂ b.

  leLtTrans po resp a≤b (b≤c , b≉c) =
    -- Step 2: transitivity of ≤₁ applied to a ≤₁ b and b ≤₁ c gives a ≤₁ c. This is the first component needed for a <₁ c.

1. [lemma/hard] In a Kleene algebra, the order is defined by a ≤ b if and only if a + b = b. This order is a partial order: it is reflexive because a + a = a by idempotence, it is antisymmetric because a ≤ b and b ≤ a give a = a + b = b + a = b by commutativity, and it is transitive by associativity. Addition is the least upper bound for this order, so b ≤ b + c for all b and c.
2. [lemma/hard] Multiplication is monotone in both arguments: if p ≤ q then r·p ≤ r·q and p·r ≤ q·r for all r. This holds because p + q = q gives r·p + r·q = r·(p + q) = r·q by distributivity, and similarly on the right.
3. [lemma/hard] For every a, the star axioms give 1 + a·a* ≤ a* and 1 + a*·a ≤ a*. Since b ≤ b + c, it follows that a·a* ≤ a* and a*·a ≤ a*.

5. [lemma/hard] If b + a·c ≤ c, then a*·b ≤ c. This is the left induction rule of the Kleene star, which says that a*·b is the least solution z of z = b + a·z.
6. [lemma/hard] If b + c·a ≤ c, then b·a* ≤ c. This is the right induction rule of the Kleene star, which says that b·a* is the least solution z of z = b + z·a.

1. [step] Throughout, + is ordinary addition on the natural numbers and ≈ is ordinary equality of natural numbers, so the claim is: if a + b = b and b + a = a, then a = b.
2. [lemma/hard] For every n, n + 0 = n. We argue by induction on n. Base case: 0 + 0 reduces to 0, so the two sides agree. Inductive case: assume n + 0 = n. Then (suc n) + 0 reduces to suc (n + 0), which by the induction hypothesis equals suc n.
3. [lemma/hard] For all m and n, m + suc n = suc (m + n). We argue by induction on m, holding n fixed. Base case: 0 + suc n reduces to suc n, and suc (0 + n) reduces to suc n, so the two sides agree. Inductive case: assume m + suc n = suc (m + n). Then (suc m) + suc n reduces to suc (m + suc n), which by the induction hypothesis equals suc (suc (m + n)), which is suc ((suc m) + n).
4. [lemma/hard] For all a and b, a + b = b + a. We argue by induction on a, holding b fixed. Base case: 0 + b reduces to b, and b + 0 equals b by the lemma plusZeroRight, so the two sides agree. Inductive case: assume a + b = b + a. Then (suc a) + b reduces to suc (a + b), which by the induction hypothesis equals suc (b + a), which by the lemma plusSucRight equals b + suc a.
5. [step] Now assume a + b = b and b + a = a. By the lemma plusComm, a + b = b + a. Combining this with the first assumption gives b = a + b, and then b = a + b = b + a = a, using the second assumption at the last equality.
6. [step] We have shown b = a. By symmetry of equality, a = b, which is the required conclusion a ≈ b.

open import Algebra.Definitions _≈_
open import Relation.Binary.Reasoning.Setoid setoid

0⋆≈1 : 0# ⋆ ≈ 1#
0⋆≈1 = begin
  0# ⋆           ≈⟨ sym (starExpansiveˡ 0#) ⟩
  1# + 0# ⋆ * 0# ≈⟨ +-congˡ ( zeroʳ (0# ⋆)) ⟩
  1# + 0#        ≈⟨ +-identityʳ 1# ⟩
  1#             ∎

1+x⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → 1# + x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
1+x⋆≈x⋆ x = sym (begin
  x ⋆                   ≈⟨ sym (starExpansiveʳ x) ⟩
  1# + x * x ⋆          ≈⟨ +-congʳ (sym (+-idem 1#)) ⟩
  1# + 1# + x * x ⋆     ≈⟨ +-assoc 1# 1# ((x * x ⋆ )) ⟩
  1# + (1# + x * x ⋆)   ≈⟨ +-congˡ (starExpansiveʳ x) ⟩
  1# + x ⋆              ∎)

x⋆+xx⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → x ⋆ + x * x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
x⋆+xx⋆≈x⋆ x = begin
  x ⋆ + x * x ⋆         ≈⟨ +-congʳ (sym (1+x⋆≈x⋆ x)) ⟩
  1# + x ⋆ + x * x ⋆    ≈⟨ +-congʳ (+-comm 1# ((x ⋆))) ⟩
  x ⋆ + 1# + x * x ⋆    ≈⟨ +-assoc ((x ⋆)) 1# ((x * x ⋆ )) ⟩
  x ⋆ + (1# + x * x ⋆)  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (starExpansiveʳ x) ⟩
  x ⋆ + x ⋆             ≈⟨ +-idem (x ⋆) ⟩
  x ⋆                   ∎

x⋆+x⋆x≈x⋆ : ∀ x → x ⋆ + x ⋆ * x ≈ x ⋆
x⋆+x⋆x≈x⋆ x = begin
  x ⋆ + x ⋆ * x         ≈⟨ +-congʳ (sym (1+x⋆≈x⋆ x)) ⟩
  1# + x ⋆ + x ⋆ * x    ≈⟨ +-congʳ (+-comm 1# (x ⋆)) ⟩
  x ⋆ + 1# + x ⋆ * x    ≈⟨ +-assoc (x ⋆) 1# (x ⋆ * x) ⟩
  x ⋆ + (1# + x ⋆ * x)  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (starExpansiveˡ x) ⟩
  x ⋆ + x ⋆             ≈⟨ +-idem (x ⋆) ⟩
  x ⋆                   ∎

x+x⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → x + x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
x+x⋆≈x⋆ x = begin
  x + x ⋆                  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (sym (starExpansiveʳ x)) ⟩
  x + (1# + x * x ⋆)       ≈⟨ +-congʳ (sym (*-identityʳ x)) ⟩
  x * 1# + (1# + x * x ⋆)  ≈⟨ sym (+-assoc (x * 1#) 1# (x * x ⋆)) ⟩
  x * 1# + 1# + x * x ⋆    ≈⟨ +-congʳ (+-comm (x * 1#) 1#) ⟩
  1# + x * 1# + x * x ⋆    ≈⟨ +-assoc 1# (x * 1#) (x * x ⋆) ⟩
  1# + (x * 1# + x * x ⋆)  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (sym (distribˡ x 1# ((x ⋆)))) ⟩
  1# + x * (1# + x ⋆)      ≈⟨ +-congˡ (*-congˡ (1+x⋆≈x⋆ x)) ⟩
  1# + x * x ⋆             ≈⟨ (starExpansiveʳ x) ⟩
  x ⋆                      ∎

1+x+x⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → 1# + x + x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
1+x+x⋆≈x⋆ x = begin
  1# + x + x ⋆    ≈⟨ +-assoc 1# x (x ⋆) ⟩
  1# + (x + x ⋆)  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (x+x⋆≈x⋆ x) ⟩
  1# + x ⋆        ≈⟨ 1+x⋆≈x⋆ x ⟩
  x ⋆             ∎

0+x+x⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → 0# + x + x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
0+x+x⋆≈x⋆ x = begin
  0# + x + x ⋆    ≈⟨ +-assoc 0# x (x ⋆) ⟩
  0# + (x + x ⋆)  ≈⟨ +-identityˡ ((x + x ⋆)) ⟩
  (x + x ⋆)       ≈⟨ x+x⋆≈x⋆ x ⟩
  x ⋆             ∎

x⋆x⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → x ⋆ * x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
x⋆x⋆≈x⋆ x = starDestructiveˡ x (x ⋆) (x ⋆) (x⋆+xx⋆≈x⋆ x)

1+x⋆x⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → 1# + x ⋆ * x ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
1+x⋆x⋆≈x⋆ x = begin
  1# + x ⋆ * x ⋆  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (x⋆x⋆≈x⋆ x) ⟩
  1# + x ⋆        ≈⟨ 1+x⋆≈x⋆ x ⟩
  x ⋆             ∎

x⋆⋆≈x⋆ : ∀ x → (x ⋆) ⋆ ≈ x ⋆
x⋆⋆≈x⋆ x = begin
  (x ⋆) ⋆        ≈⟨ sym (*-identityʳ ((x ⋆) ⋆)) ⟩
  (x ⋆) ⋆ * 1#   ≈⟨ starDestructiveˡ (x ⋆) 1# (x ⋆) (1+x⋆x⋆≈x⋆ x) ⟩
  x ⋆            ∎

1+11≈1 : 1# + 1# * 1# ≈ 1#
1+11≈1 = begin
  1# + 1# * 1#  ≈⟨ +-congˡ ( *-identityʳ 1#) ⟩
  1# + 1#       ≈⟨ +-idem 1# ⟩
  1#            ∎

1⋆≈1 : 1# ⋆ ≈ 1#
1⋆≈1 = begin
  1# ⋆       ≈⟨ sym (*-identityʳ (1# ⋆)) ⟩
  1# ⋆ * 1#  ≈⟨ starDestructiveˡ 1# 1# 1# 1+11≈1 ⟩
  1#         ∎

x≈y⇒1+xy⋆≈y⋆ : ∀ x y → x ≈  y → 1# + x * y ⋆ ≈ y ⋆
x≈y⇒1+xy⋆≈y⋆ x y eq = begin
  1# + x * y ⋆  ≈⟨ +-congˡ (*-congʳ (eq)) ⟩
  1# + y * y ⋆  ≈⟨ starExpansiveʳ y ⟩
  y ⋆           ∎

x≈y⇒x⋆≈y⋆ : ∀ x y → x ≈ y → x ⋆ ≈ y ⋆
x≈y⇒x⋆≈y⋆ x y eq = begin
  x ⋆       ≈⟨ sym (*-identityʳ (x ⋆)) ⟩
  x ⋆ * 1#  ≈⟨ (starDestructiveˡ x 1# (y ⋆) (x≈y⇒1+xy⋆≈y⋆ x y eq)) ⟩
  y ⋆       ∎

ax≈xb⇒x+axb⋆≈xb⋆ : ∀ x a b → a * x ≈ x * b → x + a * (x * b ⋆) ≈ x * b ⋆
ax≈xb⇒x+axb⋆≈xb⋆ x a b eq = begin
  x + a * (x * b ⋆)       ≈⟨ +-congˡ (sym(*-assoc a x (b ⋆))) ⟩
  x + a * x * b ⋆         ≈⟨ +-congʳ (sym (*-identityʳ x)) ⟩
  x * 1# + a * x * b ⋆    ≈⟨ +-congˡ (*-congʳ (eq)) ⟩
  x * 1# + x * b * b ⋆    ≈⟨ +-congˡ (*-assoc x b (b ⋆) ) ⟩
  x * 1# + x * (b * b ⋆)  ≈⟨ sym (distribˡ x 1# (b * b ⋆)) ⟩
  x * (1# + b * b ⋆)      ≈⟨ *-congˡ (starExpansiveʳ b) ⟩
  x * b ⋆                 ∎

-- dsp: lemmas
-- dsp: end of lemmas
plusComm : ∀ a b → a + b ≈ b + a
-- Induction on a, holding b fixed. Carrier is abstract, so no zero/suc patterns.
-- Base case: when a is zero, 0 + b reduces to b. By the lemma plusZeroRight, b + 0 equals b. So both sides equal b.
-- Inductive case: assume a + b = b + a. Then (suc a) + b reduces to suc (a + b).
-- By the induction hypothesis, suc (a + b) equals suc (b + a).
-- By the lemma plusSucRight, suc (b + a) equals b + suc a. Hence (suc a) + b equals b + suc a.
plusComm a b = (+-comm a b)

-- dsp: lemmas
plusComm : ∀ a b → a + b ≈ b + a
-- Induction on a, holding b fixed. Carrier is abstract, so no zero/suc patterns.
-- Base case: when a is zero, 0 + b reduces to b. By the lemma plusZeroRight, b + 0 equals b. So both sides equal b.
-- Inductive case: assume a + b = b + a. Then (suc a) + b reduces to suc (a + b).
-- By the induction hypothesis, suc (a + b) equals suc (b + a).
-- By the lemma plusSucRight, suc (b + a) equals b + suc a. Hence (suc a) + b equals b + suc a.
plusComm a b = (+-comm a b)

leq-antisym : ∀ a b → a + b ≈ b → b + a ≈ a → a ≈ b
-- Step 1: Assume a + b = b and b + a = a; the claim is a = b.
-- Step 5: By the lemma plusComm, a + b = b + a. Combining this with the first assumption gives b = a + b, and then b = a + b = b + a = a, using the second assumption at the last equality.
-- Step 6: We have shown b = a. By symmetry of equality, a = b, which is the required conclusion a ≈ b.
leq-antisym a b p q = (trans (sym q) (trans (plusComm b a) p))

-- dsp: end of lemmas
distribLeft : ∀ r p q → r * (p + q) ≈ r * p + r * q
-- Step 1: Left distributivity is the law itself, supplied by the semiring structure as an earlier lemma; invoke it directly.
-- Step 2: Fix arbitrary r, p and q (bound by the signature), so the earlier lemma gives r * (p + q) ≈ r * p + r * q at these values.
distribLeft r p q = (distribˡ r p q)

plusComm : ∀ a b → a + b ≈ b + a
-- Induction on a, holding b fixed. Carrier is abstract, so no zero/suc patterns.
-- Base case: when a is zero, 0 + b reduces to b. By the lemma plusZeroRight, b + 0 equals b. So both sides equal b.
-- Inductive case: assume a + b = b + a. Then (suc a) + b reduces to suc (a + b).
-- By the induction hypothesis, suc (a + b) equals suc (b + a).
-- By the lemma plusSucRight, suc (b + a) equals b + suc a. Hence (suc a) + b equals b + suc a.
plusComm a b = (+-comm a b)

leq-antisym : ∀ a b → a + b ≈ b → b + a ≈ a → a ≈ b
-- Step 1: Assume a + b = b and b + a = a; the claim is a = b.
-- Step 5: By the lemma plusComm, a + b = b + a. Combining this with the first assumption gives b = a + b, and then b = a + b = b + a = a, using the second assumption at the last equality.
-- Step 6: We have shown b = a. By symmetry of equality, a = b, which is the required conclusion a ≈ b.
leq-antisym a b p q = (trans (sym q) (trans (plusComm b a) p))

distribLeft : ∀ r p q → r * (p + q) ≈ r * p + r * q
-- Step 1: Left distributivity is the law itself, supplied by the semiring structure as an earlier lemma; invoke it directly.
-- Step 2: Fix arbitrary r, p and q (bound by the signature), so the earlier lemma gives r * (p + q) ≈ r * p + r * q at these values.
distribLeft r p q = (distribˡ r p q)

mono-left : ∀ r p q → p + q ≈ q → r * p + r * q ≈ r * q
-- Steps 1-4: Fix r, p, q with hypothesis p + q ≈ q. Using distribLeft (symmetric form), r * p + r * q ≈ r * (p + q). Multiplication by r respects ≈ in its second argument, so r * (p + q) ≈ r * q from the hypothesis. Chain by transitivity of ≈ to get r * p + r * q ≈ r * q.
mono-left r p q h = (trans (sym (distribLeft r p q)) (*-congˡ h))

1. [step] We use three facts about the magma. The relation ≈ is an equivalence relation, so it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The operation · respects ≈ in its second argument: if a ≈ b, then c · a ≈ c · b for every c.
2. [step] We prove the first implication. Let x, y, z be elements with x ≈ y and x ∤ z. We must show y ∤ z.
3. [case] Suppose, for contradiction, that y ∤ z fails. Then there is an element q with q · y ≈ z.
4. [step] Since x ≈ y, the congruence of · in its second argument gives q · x ≈ q · y.
5. [step] Combining q · x ≈ q · y with q · y ≈ z, transitivity of ≈ gives q · x ≈ z.
6. [step] This says that q is an element with q · x ≈ z, which contradicts the hypothesis x ∤ z. Hence no such q exists, so y ∤ z.
7. [step] We prove the second implication. Let x, y, z be elements with x ≈ y and z ∤ x. We must show z ∤ y.
8. [case] Suppose, for contradiction, that z ∤ y fails. Then there is an element q with q · z ≈ y.
9. [step] Since x ≈ y, symmetry of ≈ gives y ≈ x. Combining q · z ≈ y with y ≈ x, transitivity of ≈ gives q · z ≈ x.
10. [step] This says that q is an element with q · z ≈ x, which contradicts the hypothesis z ∤ x. Hence no such q exists, so z ∤ y.
11. [step] Both implications hold for all x, y, z, so the non-divisibility relation ∤ respects ≈ in its right argument and in its left argument. That is, ∤ respects ≈ in both arguments.

1. [lemma/hard] If d divides a and d divides b, then d divides a + b. Write a = d·x and b = d·y for some natural numbers x and y. Then a + b = d·x + d·y = d·(x + y) by distributivity, so d divides a + b with witness x + y.
2. [lemma/hard] If d divides m, then d divides q·m for every natural number q. Write m = d·x. Then q·m = q·(d·x) = d·(q·x) by associativity and commutativity of multiplication, so d divides q·m with witness q·x.
3. [lemma/hard] For every natural number n and every m > 0, there exist natural numbers q and r with n = q·m + r and r < m. We prove this by strong induction on n. If n < m, take q = 0 and r = n, since 0·m + n = n. If n ≥ m, then n − m is a natural number with n − m < n, because m > 0. By the induction hypothesis, n − m = q'·m + r for some q' and some r < m. Then n = (n − m) + m = (q' + 1)·m + r, so we take q = q' + 1 and this r.
4. [induction] We prove the statement by strong induction on m. The statement P(m) is: for all natural numbers n, gcd(m, n) divides m and gcd(m, n) divides n. Fix m and assume P(m') holds for every m' < m. That is, for every m' < m and every n', gcd(m', n') divides m' and gcd(m', n') divides n'. We must show P(m), so let n be an arbitrary natural number.
5. [case] Case m = 0. By the base equation of the recurrence, gcd(0, n) = n. We must show that n divides 0 and that n divides n. The first holds because 0 = n·0. The second holds because n = n·1. Hence gcd(0, n) divides both 0 and n.
6. [case] Case m > 0. By divAlg, choose q and r with n = q·m + r and r < m. By the recurrence for m > 0, gcd(m, n) = gcd(r, m), since n mod m = r. Let d = gcd(m, n), so that d = gcd(r, m).
7. [step] Since r < m, the induction hypothesis P(r) applies. It gives, for the natural number n' = m, that gcd(r, m) divides r and gcd(r, m) divides m. Since d = gcd(r, m), we have that d divides r and d divides m.
8. [step] We have shown d divides m. Since d = gcd(m, n), this is the first conjunct: gcd(m, n) divides m.

module Data.Nat.GCD where

open import Data.Nat.Base
open import Data.Nat.Divisibility
open import Data.Nat.DivMod
open import Data.Nat.GCD.Lemmas
open import Data.Nat.Properties
open import Data.Nat.Induction
  using (Acc; acc; <′-Rec; <′-recBuilder; <-wellFounded-fast)
open import Data.Product.Base
  using (_×_; _,_; proj₂; proj₁; swap; uncurry′; ∃; map)
open import Data.Sum.Base as Sum using (_⊎_; inj₁; inj₂)
open import Function.Base using (_$_; _∘_)
open import Induction using (build)
open import Induction.Lexicographic using (_⊗_; [_⊗_])
open import Relation.Binary.Definitions using (tri<; tri>; tri≈; Symmetric)
open import Relation.Binary.PropositionalEquality.Core as ≡
  using (_≡_; _≢_; subst; cong)
open import Relation.Binary.PropositionalEquality.Properties
  using (module ≡-Reasoning)
open import Relation.Nullary.Decidable.Core using (Dec)
open import Relation.Nullary.Negation.Core using (contradiction)
import Relation.Nullary.Decidable as Dec

open import Algebra.Definitions {A = ℕ} _≡_ as Algebra
  using (Associative; Commutative; LeftIdentity; RightIdentity; LeftZero; RightZero; Zero)

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Definition

-- Calculated via Euclid's algorithm. In order to show progress,
-- avoiding the initial step where the first argument may increase, it
-- is necessary to first define a version `gcd′` which assumes that the
-- second argument is strictly smaller than the first. The full `gcd`
-- function then compares the two arguments and applies `gcd′`
-- accordingly.

gcd′ : ∀ m n → Acc _<_ m → n < m → ℕ
gcd′ m zero      _         _   = m
gcd′ m n@(suc _) (acc rec) n<m = gcd′ n (m % n) (rec n<m) (m%n<n m n)

gcd : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ
gcd m n with <-cmp m n
... | tri< m<n _ _ = gcd′ n m (<-wellFounded-fast n) m<n
... | tri≈ _ _ _   = m
... | tri> _ _ n<m = gcd′ m n (<-wellFounded-fast m) n<m

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Core properties of gcd′

gcd′[m,n]∣m,n : ∀ {m n} rec n<m → gcd′ m n rec n<m ∣ m × gcd′ m n rec n<m ∣ n
gcd′[m,n]∣m,n {m} {zero}      rec       n<m = ∣-refl , m ∣0
gcd′[m,n]∣m,n {m} {n@(suc _)} (acc rec) n<m
  with gcd∣n , gcd∣m%n ← gcd′[m,n]∣m,n (rec n<m) (m%n<n m n)
  = ∣n∣m%n⇒∣m gcd∣n gcd∣m%n , gcd∣n

gcd′-greatest : ∀ {m n c} rec n<m → c ∣ m → c ∣ n → c ∣ gcd′ m n rec n<m
gcd′-greatest {m} {zero}      rec       n<m c∣m c∣n = c∣m
gcd′-greatest {m} {n@(suc _)} (acc rec) n<m c∣m c∣n =
  gcd′-greatest (rec n<m) (m%n<n m n) c∣n (%-presˡ-∣ c∣m c∣n)

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Core properties of gcd

gcd[m,n]∣m : ∀ m n → gcd m n ∣ m
gcd[m,n]∣m m n with <-cmp m n
... | tri< n<m _ _ = proj₂ (gcd′[m,n]∣m,n {n} {m} _ _)
... | tri≈ _ _ _   = ∣-refl
... | tri> _ _ m<n = proj₁ (gcd′[m,n]∣m,n {m} {n} _ _)

gcd[m,n]∣n : ∀ m n → gcd m n ∣ n
gcd[m,n]∣n m n with <-cmp m n
... | tri< n<m _    _ = proj₁ (gcd′[m,n]∣m,n {n} {m} _ _)
... | tri≈ _ ≡.refl _ = ∣-refl
... | tri> _ _    m<n = proj₂ (gcd′[m,n]∣m,n {m} {n} _ _)

gcd-greatest : ∀ {m n c} → c ∣ m → c ∣ n → c ∣ gcd m n
gcd-greatest {m} {n} c∣m c∣n with <-cmp m n
... | tri< n<m _ _ = gcd′-greatest _ _ c∣n c∣m
... | tri≈ _ _ _   = c∣m
... | tri> _ _ m<n = gcd′-greatest _ _ c∣m c∣n

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Other properties

-- Note that all other properties of `gcd` should be inferable from the
-- 3 core properties above.

gcd[n,n]≡n : ∀ n → gcd n n ≡ n
gcd[n,n]≡n n = ∣-antisym (gcd[m,n]∣m n n) (gcd-greatest ∣-refl ∣-refl)

1. [lemma/hard] If P and Q are decidable propositions, then the conjunction "P and Q" is decidable. First decide P. If P does not hold, then "P and Q" does not hold, because a proof of "P and Q" would give a proof of P. If P holds, decide Q. If Q does not hold, then "P and Q" does not hold, because a proof of "P and Q" would give a proof of Q. If Q holds, then "P and Q" holds, witnessed by the pair consisting of the proof of P and the proof of Q.
2. [lemma/hard] For vectors of length zero, the two empty vectors are pointwise related. The definition of pointwise relatedness has a case for empty vectors that imposes no condition, so this case holds.
3. [lemma/hard] Let x be in A, y be in B, and let xs and ys be vectors of the same length n. Then the vector obtained by putting x in front of xs and the vector obtained by putting y in front of ys are pointwise related if and only if x ∼ y holds and xs and ys are pointwise related. This follows from the definition of pointwise relatedness, whose case for nonempty vectors requires exactly these two facts, in both directions.
4. [step] Every vector of length zero is the empty vector. Every vector of length suc n has the form of some element x of A placed in front of some vector xs of length n. This holds because vectors are built by exactly these two constructions, and the length index determines which one applies.
5. [induction] We argue by induction on n. The statement to prove for each n is that, for all vectors xs and ys of length n, it is decidable whether xs and ys are pointwise related.
6. [case] Base case n = 0: let xs and ys be vectors of length zero. By step 4 both are the empty vector, and by lemma pointwiseNil they are pointwise related. So the decision procedure answers yes, together with this proof.
7. [case] Inductive case: assume that pointwise relatedness is decidable for vectors of length n. Let xs and ys be vectors of length suc n. By step 4, xs has the form of some x in A placed in front of some vector xs' of length n, and ys has the form of some y in B placed in front of some vector ys' of length n.
8. [case] Since the relation ∼ is decidable, decide whether x ∼ y holds.
9. [case] By the induction hypothesis, decide whether xs' and ys' are pointwise related.
10. [case] By lemma pointwiseCons, xs and ys are pointwise related if and only if x ∼ y holds and xs' and ys' are pointwise related. Applying lemma decidableConjunction to the two decisions from steps 8 and 9 gives a decision for this conjunction, together with a proof or a refutation as required.
11. [step] The procedure described in steps 6 and 10 is an algorithm, since it is built from the given decision procedure for ∼, from the decision procedure for length n, and from a constant answer in the base case. The induction therefore provides, for every n, an algorithm deciding whether two vectors of length n are pointwise related. For n = 0 the algorithm always answers yes.

1. [step] Pointwise is an inductive family indexed by two vectors of lengths n. It has two constructors: a nil constructor, which relates the empty vector to the empty vector, and a cons constructor, which relates a vector whose head is u and tail is us to a vector whose head is v and tail is vs, provided that u ∼ v and that the tails are pointwise related.
2. [case] We argue by case analysis on the given proof that Pointwise relates x ∷ xs to y ∷ ys. This proof is a term built from one of the two constructors.
3. [case] The nil constructor cannot produce this proof, because its indices are the empty vector on both sides, and the indices x ∷ xs and y ∷ ys are not empty. So this case is impossible and gives no further goal.
4. [case] The cons constructor is the only remaining possibility. Its indices are the vectors u ∷ us and v ∷ vs, and unifying them with x ∷ xs and y ∷ ys gives u = x, us = xs, v = y, and vs = ys.
5. [step] By the definition of the cons constructor, the proof of this case carries a first component which is a proof of x ∼ y, namely the relation between the heads.
6. [step] Therefore, from any proof of Pointwise relating x ∷ xs to y ∷ ys, we obtain a proof of x ∼ y, which is what was to be shown.

record Pointwise {a b ℓ} {A : Set a} {B : Set b} (_∼_ : REL A B ℓ)

                 where
  constructor ext
  field app : ∀ i → lookup xs i ∼ lookup ys i

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Operations

head : ∀ {_∼_ : REL A B ℓ} {n x y xs} {ys : Vec B n} →
       Pointwise _∼_ (x ∷ xs) (y ∷ ys) → x ∼ y
head (ext app) = app zero

tail : ∀ {_∼_ : REL A B ℓ} {n x y xs} {ys : Vec B n} →
       Pointwise _∼_ (x ∷ xs) (y ∷ ys) → Pointwise _∼_ xs ys

gmap {_∼′_ = _∼′_} ∼⇒∼′ {x ∷ xs} {y ∷ ys} xs∼ys = ext λ

  ; (suc i) → Pointwise.app (gmap {_∼′_ = _∼′_} ∼⇒∼′ (tail xs∼ys)) i
  }

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- The inductive and extensional definitions are equivalent.

module _ {_∼_ : REL A B ℓ} where

  extensional⇒inductive : ∀ {n} {xs : Vec A n} {ys : Vec B n} →

  extensional⇒inductive {xs = x ∷ xs} {y ∷ ys} xs∼ys =
    (head xs∼ys) ∷ extensional⇒inductive (tail xs∼ys)

  inductive⇒extensional : ∀ {n} {xs : Vec A n} {ys : Vec B n} →
                           IPointwise _∼_ xs ys → Pointwise _∼_ xs ys

  inductive⇒extensional (x∼y ∷ xs∼ys) = ext λ
    { zero    → x∼y
    ; (suc i) → Pointwise.app (inductive⇒extensional xs∼ys) i
    }

------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Relational properties

refl : ∀ {_∼_ : Rel A ℓ} {n} →
       Reflexive _∼_ → Reflexive (Pointwise _∼_ {n = n})

sym : ∀ {P : REL A B ℓ₁} {Q : REL B A ℓ₂} {n} →
      Sym P Q → Sym (Pointwise P) (Pointwise Q {n = n})

trans : ∀ {P : REL A B ℓ₁} {Q : REL B C ℓ₂} {R : REL A C ℓ} {n} →

pointwiseNil : ∀ {_∼_ : REL A B ℓ} → Pointwise _∼_ [] []

1. [step] Let P and Q be decidable propositions. We must show that the conjunction P and Q is decidable, that is, that we can either produce a proof of P and Q or show that no such proof exists.
2. [case] Since P is decidable, we decide P. There are two cases: P does not hold, or P holds.
3. [case] Suppose P does not hold. Then P and Q does not hold, because a proof of P and Q would contain a proof of P as its first component, which contradicts the assumption that P does not hold.
4. [case] Suppose P holds. Since Q is decidable, we decide Q. There are two cases: Q does not hold, or Q holds.
5. [case] Suppose Q does not hold. Then P and Q does not hold, because a proof of P and Q would contain a proof of Q as its second component, which contradicts the assumption that Q does not hold.
6. [case] Suppose Q holds. Together with the fact that P holds, we have a proof of P and a proof of Q, so the pair consisting of these two proofs is a proof of P and Q. Hence P and Q holds.
7. [step] In each of the four possible outcomes we have either a proof of P and Q or a demonstration that none exists. Therefore the conjunction P and Q is decidable.

Then x < y holds exactly when either len(x) < len(y), or len(x) = len(y) and x is lexicographically smaller than y, meaning that at the first position where they differ, x has 0 and y has 1. But two identical strings have no position where they differ, so there is no first differing position at which x has 0 and x has 1. Hence x ≮ x.

4. [case] Case len(x) < len(y) and len(y) ≤ len(z). If len(y) < len(z), then len(x) < len(z) and so x < z. If len(y) = len(z), then len(x) < len(z) and so x < z.
5. [case] Case len(x) = len(y) and len(y) < len(z). Then len(x) < len(z), so x < z.
6. [case] Case len(x) = len(y) = len(z). Let i be the first position where x and y differ, so x has 0 at i and y has 1 at i. Let j be the first position where y and z differ, so y has 0 at j and z has 1 at j. We cannot have i = j, since y would then have both 1 and 0 at the same position.

7. [step] For every A ∈ 𝒫_k, g(f(A)) = S∖(S∖A) = A by complementInvolutive. For every B ∈ 𝒫_{n−k}, f(g(B)) = S∖(S∖B) = B by complementInvolutive. So g is an inverse of f, and f is a bijection from 𝒫_k to 𝒫_{n−k}.
8. [step] A bijection between two finite sets shows that they have the same number of elements. So |𝒫_k| = |𝒫_{n−k}|, that is, n C′ k = n C′ (n − k). Since n − k = n ∸ k, this gives n C′ (n ∸ k) = n C′ k.
